angle: Reps got jealous of enterprise deals, emailed 40 people at one company in a week, and killed deliverability
post_first_line: 40 people at one company. One week.
linkedin_post:
40 people at one company. One week.

That's what quietly wrecked a team's deliverability.

A couple of reps on a team saw the ticket price on enterprise deals and got excited. Really excited. Some of them got jealous of the reps closing those deals.

So they started sending to 40 different people at the same large company in the same week.

The data had been fine. We had two cohorts, mid-market and enterprise, and things were going well for both. Then behavior changed, and enterprise recipients stopped receiving emails at the same rate.

The dashboards told us something broke. They didn't tell us why.

We had to open up the actual sequences and look at what changed from a sending perspective. That's where we saw it: certain sending behaviors led to a deliverability problem.

The lesson for me: when a cohort drops off, don't just stare at the metric. Compare it to the prior history where things worked, then inspect what reps actually did differently.

The cause was rep behavior, not the list or the copy.

Where have you seen rep behavior break your metrics?

Slide 2: Reps saw enterprise ticket prices and got jealous
Slide 3: Enterprise recipients stopped receiving emails like before
Slide 4: Prior data looked healthy, then behavior suddenly shifted
Slide 5: The dashboard showed the drop, not the reason why
Slide 6: We had to inspect the actual sequences being sent
Slide 7: Certain sending behaviors caused the deliverability problem
Slide 8: Compare against prior history, then check rep behavior

lesson.title: When deliverability drops, look at rep behavior
takeaways: Enterprise excitement can push reps to over-send to many contacts at one company in a short window.
Metrics show that something changed, but only inspecting actual sequences shows why.
Prior history where things went well is your baseline for spotting what changed.
lesson.exercise: Pull the last 30 days of sends for one cohort that dropped, then count how many contacts each rep emailed per account per week and compare it to a period when results were healthy.

angle: If your only email variable is first name, you have work to do.
post_first_line: Sending 10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.
linkedin_post:
Sending 10,000 identical emails is a deliverability problem.

Most people think first name fixes it. It doesn't.

Copy variation helps deliverability. You don't want the same email going out to every recipient, no matter how many people it's spread across.

So in every case, I recommend templated variables. First name. The mailboxes you're sending from. Those are the easy ones.

They should also feed into sequences with copy that uses spin syntax or is uniquely generated.

Variation beats static every time. Variables are an easy path to some degree of variation.

But here's my caveat: if your only variable is the recipient's first name, you have work to do.

What's your go-to variable beyond first name?
carousel: Slide 1: If your only email variable is first name, you have work to do.
Slide 2: Sending 10,000 of the same email hurts deliverability.
Slide 3: Variation beats static copy. Every time.
Slide 4: Template your variables: first name, sending mailbox, and more.
Slide 5: Variables are the easy path to some variation.
Slide 6: Link them to sequences with spin syntax or uniquely generated copy.
Slide 7: First name alone isn't variation. It's the bare minimum.

lesson.title: First Name Isn't Personalization: Variation for Deliverability
takeaways: Sending thousands of identical emails creates a deliverability risk, regardless of how many recipients they're spread across.
Templated variables like first name and sending mailbox are an easy way to add some variation.
Pair variables with sequences that use spin syntax or uniquely generated copy. First name alone means you have work to do.
lesson.exercise: Pull up your live sequence. Count the variables in it. If first name is the only one, add at least one more and rewrite one email using spin syntax or uniquely generated copy.

angle: Who should own what when your cold email program starts slipping
post_first_line: Four teams own cold email health.
linkedin_post:
Four teams own cold email health.
Most companies assign it to none of them.

When replies start slipping, everyone points at everyone else. Here's the split I'd use.

Sales owns the sending plan. That means how many emails go out and, at the rep level, how we ramp people up to full volume.

RevOps owns list quality. Make sure the people you're sending to have legitimate mailboxes. When replies drop, RevOps should be able to inspect which segments are actually taking the hit.

IT owns domain setup. Are your domains authenticated properly and set up to send? IT can also answer the question: what changed?

Then there's the sending vendor. Someone has to check who is sending from which domains and whether those domains are healthy. That could be RevOps, or maybe you have deliverability in-house.

When each piece has an owner, a reply drop becomes a diagnosis instead of a blame game.

Who owns deliverability at your company today?
carousel: Slide 1: Four teams own cold email health. Most companies assign none.
Slide 2: Sales owns the sending plan: volume and rep-level ramp.
Slide 3: RevOps owns list quality: legitimate mailboxes only.
Slide 4: When replies drop, RevOps inspects which segments are affected.
Slide 5: IT owns domain setup and proper authentication.
Slide 6: IT also answers the question: what changed?
Slide 7: Someone must check which domains send, and if they're healthy.
Slide 8: Clear owners turn a reply drop into a diagnosis.

lesson.title: Who Owns What When Cold Email Slips
takeaways: Sales owns the sending plan: email volume and how reps ramp to full volume.
RevOps owns list quality and should be able to inspect which segments show reply drops; IT owns domain setup and authentication, and can answer what changed.
Someone must own the sending vendor: who sends from which domains and whether those domains are healthy. That could be RevOps or in-house deliverability.
lesson.exercise: Write down the four areas (sending plan, list quality, domain setup, sending vendor) and put one named owner next to each. Any blank is where your next reply drop will stall.

caption: Who owns cold email?

angle: New mailbox, reply rates tanked. You probably started sending too soon.
linkedin_post:
New mailbox. Reply rates tanked.

The cause is usually simpler than people think.

When reply rates drop on fresh mailboxes, I start with one hypothesis: we started sending too soon.

The quality of the mailbox didn't match the aspirational target of our sending volume.

I know people have pipeline targets. But this is a deliverability problem, and more volume won't fix it.

The fix is quick. Warm the mailboxes further, ramp actual sends more slowly, and adjust from there.

Modify your daily sending volume first. Then look at everything else.

What's your rule for ramping a new mailbox?
carousel: Slide 1: New mailbox, reply rates tanked. Check this first.
Slide 2: Maybe you just started sending too soon.
Slide 3: Mailbox quality didn't match your aspirational sending target.
Slide 4: Pipeline targets don't change how deliverability works.
Slide 5: Adjust your daily sending volume first.
Slide 6: Warm the mailboxes further before sending more.
Slide 7: Ramp your actual sends more slowly.
Slide 8: Then adjust from there.

lesson.title: When a New Mailbox Underperforms, Slow Down
takeaways: Tanked reply rates on new mailboxes can simply mean you started sending too soon.
The gap is often between mailbox quality and your aspirational sending target.
The quick fix is to warm the mailboxes further and ramp sends more slowly.
lesson.exercise: Pull the daily send volume for your newest mailboxes. Cut it back, keep warming, and raise volume in small steps while tracking reply rates.

caption: Started sending too soon?

angle: 3 things to do this week to find out why your replies dropped
linkedin_post:
3 things to do this week.

If your reply rates dropped, start here before you rewrite everything.

First, pull up one email, or a couple. Check how many of the faux pas are in there. Count the links. Look at how much of the copy adds no value.

Second, run one split test against an existing sequence. Take your lead list, split it in half, and test the change. One test, one sequence.

Third, decide who owns the investigation when a drop happens. Name one person.

The drop alone won't tell you the full story. You have to see what changed at the same time as the drop.

Most teams skip that last step, and it's the one that makes the other two useful.

Who owns reply rate investigations on your team?
carousel: Slide 1: Reply rates dropped? Do these 3 things this week.
Slide 2: Step 1: Review one or two of your emails.
Slide 3: Count the links and the faux pas in the copy.
Slide 4: Cut copy that adds no value for the reader.
Slide 5: Step 2: Split test against an existing sequence.
Slide 6: Split your lead list in half and run the test.
Slide 7: Step 3: Name one owner for every drop investigation.
Slide 8: A drop alone won't tell you what actually changed.

lesson.title: How to Investigate a Drop in Replies
takeaways: Audit your emails for faux pas, too many links, and copy that adds little value.
Split your lead list in half and run one split test against an existing sequence.
Assign an owner for investigations, because the drop alone doesn't explain what changed.
lesson.exercise: Open one live email today and count the links and the lines that add no value. Then split your lead list in half and set up one split test on that sequence.

caption: Replies dropped? Do this.

angle: Same 10,000 emails, 36 meetings vs 28: what inbox placement costs you
linkedin_post:
8 meetings. Same 10,000 emails.

The only thing that changed was where the emails landed.

Take an illustrative example. One team gets a 90% placement rate, meaning emails reach the primary tab and the inbox. Based on some reply rate assumptions, 10,000 emails turn into 36 meetings.

Now change one variable: the percentage of emails that reach the recipient's inbox in the first place. Same 10,000 sent, same copy, same list. That team books 28 meetings.

That's a delta of 8 meetings.

Depending on your price point, that gap could be hundreds of thousands of ARR that never converts into deals.

Fewer emails in the inbox means fewer meetings and less revenue. Most teams I talk to optimize subject lines and copy while the real leak sits upstream.

When did you last check your inbox placement?
carousel: Slide 1: Same 10,000 emails. 36 meetings versus 28.
Slide 2: The difference isn't copy, list, or offer.
Slide 3: It's how many emails reach the inbox.
Slide 4: Team A: 90% placement, 10,000 sent, 36 meetings.
Slide 5: Team B: lower placement, same send, 28 meetings.
Slide 6: That's an 8-meeting gap from placement alone.
Slide 7: At the right price point, that's hundreds of thousands in ARR.
Slide 8: Fewer emails in the inbox means less revenue.

lesson.title: Inbox placement is a revenue lever
takeaways: Fewer emails reaching the inbox means fewer meetings and less revenue.
In the illustrative example, 10,000 emails produced 36 meetings at 90% placement versus 28 with lower placement.
An 8-meeting gap can represent hundreds of thousands of ARR, depending on price point.
lesson.exercise: Take your last 10,000 sends and your reply-to-meeting rates, then model how many meetings you'd lose if placement dropped. Multiply the gap by your average deal size.
